risks.statement: Use of untrusted or compromised LLMs
risks.description: This risk arises when LLMs obtained from untrusted or insufficiently vetted sources have been intentionally poisoned or backdoored during training or distribution, causing them to behave maliciously or unpredictably under specific conditions. controls.statement: Use only LLMs from verified and trusted model developers

controls.statement: Use only established and verified model loaders in production environments

controls.statement: Require explicit human confirmation before executing high-impact or irreversible tool actions
controls.recommendations: Agents may incorrectly select or misuse high-impact tools, leading to irreversible damage such as data deletion, unauthorised financial transactions, or unintended system modifications. Implement mandatory human-in-the-loop approval workflows for tools that perform high-impact or irreversible actions, including sending external communications, executing financial transactions, deleting or modifying critical data, and making privileged configuration changes. Configure approval interfaces to clearly display the tool being invoked, the parameters being passed, and the expected outcome, enabling informed human decision-making. Ensure approval mechanisms cannot be bypassed by agents and maintain audit logs of all approval decisions, including who approved what action and when. Approval steps decay under volume: in one large deployment users approved about 93% of permission prompts. Pair this control with CTRL-0094 - measure approval and override rates, route routine actions to automated screening, and reserve human approval for genuinely uncertain or high-impact actions so that the approvals that remain are real decisions.
controls.evidence: The tool registry marking each irreversible tool as confirmation-required, and the audit log recording who confirmed which tool call, with parameters and time.
controls.test: Invoke a tool marked irreversible through the tool layer without a confirmation record and confirm the call is refused and logged.

controls.statement: Conduct safety verification with domain-relevant stress tests and adversarial scenarios before deployment and on a regular cadence afterwards
controls.recommendations: Deploying agents without rigorous safety testing risks exposing users to harmful behaviours, security vulnerabilities, or compliance violations that only emerge under adversarial or edge-case conditions. Document test results, identified vulnerabilities, and implemented mitigations for future reference and regular review. Repeat the exercise on a fixed cadence and whenever the model, tools, or capabilities change - attacks evolve faster than deployments. Use established agent security and safety benchmarks (for example AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, and AgentHarm) as a baseline and add scenarios drawn from your own incidents and from published ones.

controls.test: Run AgentDojo, AgentHarm and the system's own domain scenarios against the release candidate and confirm the results meet the recorded pass criteria.

risks.statement: Weak tool authentication and authorisation controls
risks.description: This risk arises when tools connected to an agent lack robust authentication or fine-grained authorisation mechanisms, allowing unauthorised access or misuse of tool capabilities. As a result, attackers or misbehaving agents may compromise the system by invoking sensitive actions, escalating privileges, or manipulating external resources beyond intended boundaries.

controls.statement: Use only tool servers and APIs, including MCP servers, that implement robust authentication mechanisms in production environments
controls.recommendations: Weak or misconfigured authorisation on the servers and APIs that an agent's tools call can lead to unauthorised access, token theft, or privilege escalation that compromises connected systems. Before deployment, verify that every remote tool endpoint authenticates its caller with a standard mechanism (for example OAuth 2.1, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, or mutually authenticated TLS) and enforces per-client scopes, and reject endpoints that rely on hard-coded credentials, unscoped shared keys, or deprecated authentication methods; test the authorisation flows in a development environment to confirm them. For MCP servers, also verify per-client consent flows and redirect URI validation to prevent authorisation bypasses, and reject servers with insufficient session management. As of the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, verify additionally that the server implements RFC 9207 issuer identification (so a client can detect a substituted authorization server) and Client ID Metadata Documents in place of dynamic client registration, and prefer servers that support the Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension so that access is governed by your identity provider rather than by per-user ad-hoc consent. Treat servers still built on the pre-2026 stateful session model as needing review before production use.
controls.evidence: The tool endpoint inventory recording each remote server's authentication mechanism and per-client scopes, with the integration review that exercised its authorisation flow.
controls.test: Call each production tool endpoint with no credential and with a credential scoped for a different client, and confirm both are refused.

risks.statement: Lack of proper role-based access control for tools
risks.description: This risk arises when tools exposed to an agent do not enforce clear, role-based access controls, allowing agents to access capabilities or resources beyond their intended responsibilities. As a result, agents may perform unauthorised actions, misuse sensitive tools, or exceed their permitted scope, increasing the likelihood of security and operational failures.

controls.statement: Limit token scopes to the minimum privileges required and avoid broad or wildcard scopes
controls.recommendations: Overly broad token scopes enable compromised or malicious actors to access resources beyond what is necessary for legitimate operations, amplifying the impact of security breaches. Define granular, task-specific scopes for each MCP server integration and request only the minimum permissions required for the intended functionality (e.g., "read:inventory" rather than "admin:*"). Review and document the justification for each requested scope during integration, and reject MCP servers that require unnecessarily broad permissions or fail to support fine-grained scope definitions. Periodically audit active token scopes to identify and revoke excessive permissions that may have accumulated over time.
controls.evidence: The OAuth client configuration listing each scope requested per tool integration with its justification, containing no wildcard or administrator scope.
controls.test: Decode a token issued to the agent in production, confirm its scopes match the configured list, then call an out-of-scope operation and confirm refusal.

risks.statement: Tool poisoning by malicious actors
risks.description: This risk arises when a tool server or agent that another party builds or operates describes itself in a way that manipulates the agent that connects to it. Instructions can be hidden in tool descriptions, parameter schemas, or agent cards; a tool can imitate or shadow a trusted one; and a definition can change after it was approved. The agent reads these descriptions as part of its instructions, so it may follow them even when the tool is never called. As a result, the agent may unknowingly execute malicious actions, leak sensitive information, or produce manipulated outputs that undermine system integrity and trust.

controls.statement: Test all untested MCP servers in a sandboxed environment before deploying to production
controls.recommendations: Untested MCP servers may contain vulnerabilities, malicious code, or unexpected behaviours that could compromise your production systems or data. Deploy MCP servers first to an isolated sandbox environment (e.g., containerised test environment, separate network segment, or dedicated development infrastructure) to evaluate their security posture, behaviour, and reliability. Monitor server activity during testing for anomalous network connections, excessive resource consumption, unauthorised file access, or other suspicious behaviours. Only promote MCP servers to production after successful security review, functional testing, and verification that the server behaves as documented.
controls.evidence: The sandbox test report for each MCP server, recording observed network connections, file access and resource use, with the promotion approval.
controls.test: Add an MCP server with no sandbox test report to the production configuration and confirm the release review rejects it.

controls.statement: Require verified provenance for tools, skills, and dependencies, and re-verify them on every update
controls.recommendations: Treat tools, MCP servers, agent skills or plug-ins, prompt templates, and packages as supply chain artefacts. Install them only from vetted registries, pin them by version and content hash, verify signatures or attestations where available, and keep an inventory (an AI bill of materials) of what each agent can load. Because approval does not survive an update, re-verify hashes and signatures at load time and diff tool definitions against the approved version so a silently changed server is detected before it runs. Do not let agents install unpinned dependencies autonomously, scan new packages for typosquatting and known vulnerabilities, and keep a way to revoke a specific tool or skill across all deployments quickly. Before adopting a tool server, skill or package, assess who publishes it: whether the code is public, how the publisher handles security disclosures, and whether it is actively maintained.

controls.statement: Define clearly the agent's role, scope, and non-goals in the system prompt
controls.recommendations: Ambiguous or missing role definitions allow agents to interpret requests too broadly, potentially executing actions outside intended boundaries or misunderstanding their authority and constraints. Explicitly define the agent's purpose, permitted actions, and operational boundaries in the system prompt, including clear statements about what the agent should not do or attempt. Document specific examples of in-scope and out-of-scope behaviours to reduce ambiguity and guide the agent's decision-making in edge cases. Regularly review and refine these definitions based on observed agent behaviour, ensuring role boundaries remain aligned with evolving use cases and risk tolerances.

controls.statement: Define clear success criteria for the agent's tasks

risks.statement: Unsanitised inputs in system instructions
risks.description: This risk arises when untrusted or user-controlled inputs are incorporated into system instructions without proper sanitisation or validation. As a result, malicious or malformed content may manipulate the model's behaviour, override intended constraints, or trigger unintended actions.

controls.statement: Keep untrusted inputs out of system instructions, and enclose any untrusted content given to the model in delimiters marked as data
controls.recommendations: Prompt injection attacks exploit LLMs' inability to distinguish between instructions and data, allowing malicious users to embed commands within input that override intended behaviour. Do not interpolate user input, retrieved content, or tool outputs into the system prompt or other instruction templates; fix the system prompt at build time and pass untrusted content to the model in the user or tool turns, where it carries less authority. Where untrusted content must be quoted, enclose it within clearly marked boundaries (e.g., XML tags or special markers) that are unlikely to appear naturally in the input, and instruct the LLM to treat delimited content as data rather than instructions. Neither measure is a complete defence, because the model can still follow instructions in untrusted content, so combine them with controls that do not depend on the model's compliance, such as a deterministic policy layer (CTRL-0090) and least privilege (CTRL-0029).
controls.evidence: The prompt-assembly code showing a fixed system prompt with no interpolated variables and a wrapper that places untrusted content inside tagged data blocks.

controls.statement: Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions

risks.statement: Poisoned memory
risks.description: This risk arises when the memory component of an agentic system is intentionally or inadvertently populated with malicious, misleading, or corrupted information. As a result, the agent may rely on compromised memory to make decisions, propagate false information, or exhibit persistent unsafe behaviour across interactions.

controls.statement: Implement allowlists and denylists to restrict what categories of information can be written to the agent's persistent memory
controls.recommendations: Unrestricted writes to persistent memory enable attackers to poison agent memory with malicious instructions, false information, or sensitive data that could compromise future agent behaviour or leak confidential information. Define explicit allowlists of permitted memory categories (e.g., user preferences, conversation context, task history) and denylists of forbidden content (e.g., credentials, system instructions, security policies, prompt overrides). Enforce these restrictions at the memory write interface, validating all write operations against the defined policies before persisting data.

controls.statement: Log all modifications to persistent memory with comprehensive source metadata for audit purposes
controls.recommendations: Without detailed audit logs, detecting and investigating memory poisoning attacks becomes extremely difficult, preventing effective incident response and forensic analysis. risks.statement: Cascading errors in multi-agent architectures
risks.description: This risk arises when errors or misjudgements produced by one agent propagate through interconnected agents within a multi-agent system. As a result, small failures may compound across agent interactions, leading to amplified errors, degraded system performance, or unintended outcomes at the system level.

controls.statement: Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
controls.recommendations: Unstructured or inadequately validated inter-agent messages create vulnerability to injection attacks, misinterpretation, and parsing errors that could compromise agent behaviour or cascade through multi-agent systems. Define explicit message schemas using formal specification languages (e.g., JSON Schema, Protobuf, OpenAPI) that specify required fields, data types, validation rules, and permitted value ranges for all agent-to-agent communications. Implement strict input validation that verifies all incoming messages conform to expected schemas, checking field presence, data types, value ranges, and structural integrity before processing message content. Reject messages that are incomplete, contain unexpected fields, violate type constraints, or include suspicious patterns, returning explicit error responses to the sending agent and logging validation failures to enable detection of compromised or malfunctioning agents.
controls.evidence: The inter-agent message schemas in version control and the validator invoked at each agent's message entry point.
controls.test: Send an agent a message with a missing required field and an undeclared extra field and confirm it returns an error and logs a validation failure.

controls.statement: Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
controls.recommendations: Unencrypted inter-agent communications expose sensitive data, credentials, and operational context to network-based attackers through eavesdropping or man-in-the-middle attacks. Ensure all agent-to-agent network communications use transport-layer encryption (minimum TLS 1.2, preferably TLS 1.3), including internal traffic within trusted network boundaries, as internal networks are increasingly targeted by sophisticated attackers. For protocol-based frameworks (e.g., A2A Protocol), verify that TLS is enabled by default; for application frameworks (e.g., LangGraph, CrewAI), configure deployment infrastructure to enforce HTTPS endpoints for all remote agent APIs. Configure agents to reject plaintext connections and verify certificates to prevent downgrade attacks or rogue agent impersonation, and regularly audit network traffic to detect agents attempting unencrypted communication.

controls.statement: Assign each agent a unique, verifiable identity with no shared credentials
controls.recommendations: Shared credentials prevent accurate attribution of agent actions, making it impossible to identify which agent performed unauthorised activities or to revoke access for compromised agents without affecting legitimate ones. Assign each agent instance a unique identity (e.g., service account, API key, certificate) that can be independently tracked, audited, and revoked without impacting other agents. Prohibit credential sharing between agents even when they perform similar functions, as unique identities enable granular access control and forensic analysis of agent behaviour. Emerging agentic IAM platforms, such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, can help to provide purpose-built identity management for AI agents. Concrete mechanisms now exist: SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identities with short rotation for agents and MCP servers, Microsoft Entra Agent ID (assigned to all new Copilot Studio agents since July 2026), and the IETF drafts for OAuth on-behalf-of delegation and transaction tokens that carry separate actor (agent) and principal (initiating human) claims; A2A v1.0 signed agent cards provide the equivalent for agent-to-agent interactions. Prefer identities that keep the delegating human visible in every token so that actions remain attributable.
controls.evidence: The identity provider's list of agent service accounts or workload identities, showing one per agent instance and no key shared between two.
controls.test: Revoke one agent's credential and confirm only that agent loses access, and that the audit log attributes its earlier actions to it alone.

controls.statement: Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
controls.recommendations: Unencrypted inter-agent communications expose sensitive data, credentials, and operational context to network-based attackers through eavesdropping or man-in-the-middle attacks. Ensure all agent-to-agent network communications use transport-layer encryption (minimum TLS 1.2, preferably TLS 1.3), including internal traffic within trusted network boundaries, as internal networks are increasingly targeted by sophisticated attackers. For protocol-based frameworks (e.g., A2A Protocol), verify that TLS is enabled by default; for application frameworks (e.g., LangGraph, CrewAI), configure deployment infrastructure to enforce HTTPS endpoints for all remote agent APIs. Configure agents to reject plaintext connections and verify certificates to prevent downgrade attacks or rogue agent impersonation, and regularly audit network traffic to detect agents attempting unencrypted communication.
controls.evidence: The service mesh or load balancer configuration requiring TLS 1.2 or higher on every agent endpoint, with plaintext listeners disabled.

controls.recommendations: Users may treat agent-generated content as completely reliable without recognising that LLMs can produce inaccurate or fabricated information presented as fact. Implement clear UI/UX indicators that remind users of hallucination risks, such as disclaimers on agent responses, visual cues distinguishing generated content from verified information, or warnings when agents make factual claims without citations. Consider contextual warnings that appear when agents discuss topics particularly prone to hallucination, such as recent events beyond the model's training data or highly specialised technical subjects.

controls.statement: Implement features enabling users to verify generated answers against source content
controls.recommendations: Without verification mechanisms, users cannot easily check whether agent-generated information is accurate or fabricated, increasing reliance on potentially hallucinated content. Provide built-in features that enable users to verify agent responses against original source materials, such as inline citations linking to specific documents or passages, source attribution showing which materials informed the response, or side-by-side views displaying retrieved content alongside generated summaries. Design verification features to minimise friction whilst maintaining effectiveness — users should be able to check sources with minimal effort rather than requiring extensive navigation or manual searching. For example, automatically highlight passages in source documents that support specific claims made by the agent, enabling rapid verification of factual statements.
controls.evidence: The response payload schema carrying source identifiers and passage offsets, and the interface code that renders them as inline citations.
controls.test: Ask a question answered by a known document and confirm each citation opens that document at the passage supporting the claim.

risks.statement: Generation of copyrighted content
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent generates content that reproduces or closely resembles copyrighted material without appropriate rights or attribution. As a result, the system may infringe intellectual property laws, expose the organisation to legal liability, or violate licensing and usage terms.

controls.statement: Implement input guardrails to detect and decline requests to generate copyrighted content
controls.recommendations: Agents may generate content that reproduces or closely resembles copyrighted material without authorisation, exposing the organisation to intellectual property infringement claims, legal liability, or licensing violations. Deploy input guardrails that detect requests asking the agent to reproduce copyrighted works such as song lyrics, book passages, proprietary code, or other protected content. Configure the system to decline these requests with appropriate messaging that explains copyright limitations and suggests legal alternatives such as summarisation, licensed access, or original creation. Note that copyright detection at the input stage may not catch all violations, as users might phrase requests in ways that obscure copyrighted content generation — tools such as Patronus AI's CopyrightCatcher can provide output-level copyright detection to complement input filtering.

controls.test: Request the full lyrics of a current chart song and a chapter of an in-copyright novel and confirm both are declined with a lawful alternative offered.

risks.statement: Inaccurate promises or statements in official communications
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent makes commitments, assurances, or public statements that are incorrect, unsupported, or exceed the organisation’s actual intentions or capabilities. As a result, the organisation may face reputational damage, legal exposure, or loss of public trust due to unmet expectations or misinformation.

controls.statement: Require human approval for communications on sensitive matters
controls.recommendations: Agents making unsupported commitments, inaccurate assurances, or statements that exceed organisational capabilities in official communications may expose the organisation to reputational damage, legal liability, or unmet expectations. Implement mandatory human review and approval workflows for communications on sensitive matters including contractual commitments, financial promises, policy statements, regulatory responses, or public-facing announcements. Define clear criteria for what constitutes "sensitive matters" requiring approval, ensuring consistent application across the organisation. Enforce the approval in the sending path, so that the agent cannot dispatch a message in a sensitive category until it is approved; an instruction to the agent to seek approval is not enough. controls.statement: Measure the quality of human oversight and redesign approval steps that have become rubber stamps
controls.recommendations: A human approval step is only a control while the human is actually deciding. Instrument approval workflows: track approval rates, response times, and override rates per user and per action type, and audit random samples of approved actions. Approval rates near 100% or response times of seconds indicate that the step has stopped working. Respond by routing only genuinely uncertain or high-impact actions to humans, screening routine ones automatically, presenting the context needed to decide (what will change, why the agent chose it, what it would cost to reverse), and training overseers on the agent's failure modes. Report oversight metrics alongside the agent's other operating metrics so that erosion is visible to the governance team.

risks.statement: Unauthorised execution of business transactions
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent initiates, authorises, or executes business transactions outside predefined approval thresholds, roles, or authorisation limits. As a result, the organisation may be exposed to unintended financial losses, binding contractual obligations, or operational commitments that were not properly sanctioned.

controls.statement: Require explicit human confirmation before committing any business transaction outside limits that an accountable human has pre-authorised
controls.recommendations: Agents executing business transactions without proper authorisation may create unintended financial obligations, contractual commitments, or operational liabilities. Have an accountable human set the limits within which the agent may transact without confirmation — for example amounts, counterparties, transaction types, and frequency — and enforce those limits outside the agent, such as in the transaction controller (CTRL-0058) or payment gateway. Pause any transaction outside the limits, and every transaction where no limits have been set, immediately before it is initiated, presenting the transaction type, amount, counterparty, and consequences for review by the user on whose behalf the agent acts or by a designated approver. Require active consent, using an explicit "confirm" action rather than a dismissible notification or opt-out. Ensure confirmation cannot be bypassed by agents, and keep audit logs of all approvals, including timestamp, approver identity, and transaction details. Pair this control with CTRL-0094 so that confirmations remain real decisions.
controls.evidence: The transaction limits signed by the accountable owner, their configuration in the transaction controller, and the confirmation log with approver identity and transaction details.
controls.test: Propose a transaction above the pre-authorised amount and confirm the controller holds it until the user actively confirms the amount and counterparty.

controls.statement: Use structured retrieval APIs for web searches rather than web scraping

Use structured retrieval APIs such as search engine APIs, knowledge bases, or curated data sources that provide pre-processed, sanitised content rather than raw web pages. Structured APIs typically return controlled formats (JSON, XML) containing extracted information without rendering full web content, reducing exposure to injection vectors embedded in HTML, CSS, or JavaScript.

controls.statement: Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions
controls.recommendations: Classifier-based injection guardrails are probabilistic and do not close the attack. Complement them with an architectural boundary in which untrusted content never directly drives privileged actions - for example a privileged planner that never sees raw untrusted data working with a quarantined model that extracts values from it (the dual-LLM pattern), capability or information-flow labels that follow data through the system, and a policy engine that checks each tool call against what the data it depends on is allowed to do. Published designs such as CaMeL, Progent, and related reference monitors largely eliminate injection success on agent benchmarks; adopt one, or an equivalent policy layer in your framework, for systems that combine untrusted content with sensitive data or consequential actions.
controls.evidence: The policy engine's rules in version control stating which tools accept data carrying each trust label, and its log of denied tool calls.
controls.test: Run AgentDojo with the policy layer enabled and confirm instructions injected into tool outputs trigger no privileged tool call.

controls.statement: Enforce default-deny network egress for agent runtimes, allowing only approved destinations
controls.recommendations: Every exfiltration and every containment escape needs an outbound channel, and agents acquire new ones with each tool. Run agent runtimes behind an egress policy that denies all outbound connections by default and allows only named destinations required for the task, applied at the network layer (proxy, firewall, or sandbox policy) rather than in the prompt. Include browsing and API tools in the policy, block requests that carry data in URLs or headers to unapproved hosts, and validate at the egress boundary that any credential presented belongs to the deployment — an allowlisted API endpoint is still an exfiltration channel if the agent can use it with an attacker's account. Log and alert on denied connections; they are an early signal of injection or misbehaviour.
controls.evidence: The egress proxy or firewall rule set for the agent runtime showing default deny and the named permitted destinations, with alerts on denied connections.
controls.test: From inside the agent runtime, request an unlisted host and call a permitted API with another account's key, and confirm both are refused and alerted.

controls.statement: Do not give one agent untrusted content, access to sensitive data, and an unrestricted outbound channel at once; remove one, or gate the outbound channel outside the agent
controls.recommendations: An agent that reads content from outside parties, can reach sensitive data, and can send data out can be turned into an exfiltration channel by a single injected instruction, and detection alone does not reliably stop this. Map, for each agent, where its inputs come from, what sensitive data it can reach, and every channel through which it can send data out, including messages, API calls, and URLs it can fetch or render. Where all three are present, break the combination: give the untrusted content to a separate agent that has no access to sensitive data and returns only structured values (see CTRL-0020 and CTRL-0090); remove the sensitive data the task does not need (see CTRL-0082); or restrict the outbound channel outside the agent, by limiting recipients and destinations to a fixed allowlist (see CTRL-0089) and requiring human approval for any message or call that carries data to a new recipient. Record which of the three is removed or gated for each agent, and recheck the map whenever a tool, data source, or channel is added. An agent that lacks any of the three does not need this control; record the waiver with evidence of which one is absent.
controls.evidence: The per-agent map of untrusted inputs, reachable sensitive data and outbound channels, recording which of the three is removed or gated, dated after the latest tool change.
controls.test: Plant an instruction in content the agent reads telling it to send a seeded secret to a new recipient and confirm the secret never leaves.

controls.statement: Provide comprehensive descriptions for each tool including intended use, required inputs, and potential outputs
controls.recommendations: Incomplete or ambiguous tool descriptions lead agents to misunderstand tool capabilities, misuse tools for unintended purposes, or select inappropriate tools for tasks, resulting in failures or unsafe behaviour. Document each tool with clear, comprehensive descriptions that specify the tool's intended purpose, required input parameters with data types and constraints, expected outputs and formats, and any preconditions or side effects. Include usage examples and common failure scenarios to guide agent decision-making and prevent misuse. Ensure tool descriptions are accurate, up-to-date, and written in language that LLMs can reliably interpret, avoiding ambiguity that might lead to incorrect tool selection or invocation.

controls.statement: Run agent-generated code only in isolated compute environments with network access blocked by default

risks.statement: Unintended overwriting or deletion of files or data
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent modifies, overwrites, or deletes files, database tables, or datasets without explicit user instruction or authorisation. As a result, critical information may be lost or corrupted, leading to data integrity issues, operational disruption, or the need for costly recovery efforts.

controls.statement: Do not grant write access to agents unless strictly necessary
controls.recommendations: Agents with unnecessary write access may inadvertently modify, overwrite, or delete critical files or data, leading to data loss, corruption, or operational disruption. Apply the principle of least privilege by granting write access only when explicitly required for the agent's intended functionality, defaulting to read-only access for all other operations. Implement granular access controls that restrict write permissions to specific directories, databases, or resources that the agent legitimately needs to modify. Regularly review agent permissions to ensure write access remains justified and revoke unnecessary permissions as agent responsibilities evolve.
controls.evidence: The agent's database grants and storage policies showing read-only access by default, with each write permission scoped to a named resource and justified.
controls.test: Using the agent's credentials, attempt a write to a table or directory outside its listed write scope and confirm it is denied.

controls.statement: Require human approval for destructive changes to databases, tables, or files that cannot be readily undone
controls.recommendations: Destructive operations such as deleting files, dropping database tables, or overwriting critical data can cause irreversible damage if executed without proper authorisation. Require human approval for every destructive operation that cannot be readily undone, including DROP and TRUNCATE statements, DELETE or UPDATE queries that are not narrowly filtered, bulk file deletions, and any deletion or overwrite in a store without versioning, soft-delete, or point-in-time recovery (see CTRL-0077). Changes that can be reverted from version control or soft-delete, such as edits to files in a version-controlled working copy, may proceed without approval. Enforce the approval in the tool or database permission layer rather than by instructing the agent to ask first, because an instruction in the agent's context can be ignored or lost.
controls.evidence: The tool or database permission rules marking DROP, TRUNCATE, unfiltered DELETE or UPDATE and bulk file deletion as approval-required, with approval records.
controls.test: Have the agent issue a DROP TABLE and an unfiltered DELETE in staging and confirm neither runs until a human approves it.

controls.statement: Measure the quality of human oversight and redesign approval steps that have become rubber stamps
controls.recommendations: A human approval step is only a control while the human is actually deciding. Instrument approval workflows: track approval rates, response times, and override rates per user and per action type, and audit random samples of approved actions. Approval rates near 100% or response times of seconds indicate that the step has stopped working. Respond by routing only genuinely uncertain or high-impact actions to humans, screening routine ones automatically, presenting the context needed to decide (what will change, why the agent chose it, what it would cost to reverse), and training overseers on the agent's failure modes. Report oversight metrics alongside the agent's other operating metrics so that erosion is visible to the governance team.
controls.evidence: The oversight metrics report giving approval rate, response time and override rate per approver and action type, with results of sampled approval audits.
controls.test: Seed the approval queue with a clearly wrong action and confirm the approver rejects it and the outcome appears in the oversight report.

controls.statement: Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions
controls.recommendations: Classifier-based injection guardrails are probabilistic and do not close the attack. Complement them with an architectural boundary in which untrusted content never directly drives privileged actions - for example a privileged planner that never sees raw untrusted data working with a quarantined model that extracts values from it (the dual-LLM pattern), capability or information-flow labels that follow data through the system, and a policy engine that checks each tool call against what the data it depends on is allowed to do. Published designs such as CaMeL, Progent, and related reference monitors largely eliminate injection success on agent benchmarks; adopt one, or an equivalent policy layer in your framework, for systems that combine untrusted content with sensitive data or consequential actions.
controls.evidence: The policy engine's rules in version control stating which tools accept data carrying each trust label, and its log of denied tool calls.
controls.test: Run AgentDojo with the policy layer enabled and confirm instructions injected into tool outputs trigger no privileged tool call.

controls.statement: Do not give one agent untrusted content, access to sensitive data, and an unrestricted outbound channel at once; remove one, or gate the outbound channel outside the agent
controls.recommendations: An agent that reads content from outside parties, can reach sensitive data, and can send data out can be turned into an exfiltration channel by a single injected instruction, and detection alone does not reliably stop this. Map, for each agent, where its inputs come from, what sensitive data it can reach, and every channel through which it can send data out, including messages, API calls, and URLs it can fetch or render. Where all three are present, break the combination: give the untrusted content to a separate agent that has no access to sensitive data and returns only structured values (see CTRL-0020 and CTRL-0090); remove the sensitive data the task does not need (see CTRL-0082); or restrict the outbound channel outside the agent, by limiting recipients and destinations to a fixed allowlist (see CTRL-0089) and requiring human approval for any message or call that carries data to a new recipient. Record which of the three is removed or gated for each agent, and recheck the map whenever a tool, data source, or channel is added. An agent that lacks any of the three does not need this control; record the waiver with evidence of which one is absent.
controls.evidence: The per-agent map of untrusted inputs, reachable sensitive data and outbound channels, recording which of the three is removed or gated, dated after the latest tool change.
controls.test: Plant an instruction in content the agent reads telling it to send a seeded secret to a new recipient and confirm the secret never leaves.

risks.statement: Data exfiltration through combined access to untrusted content, sensitive data, and an outbound channel
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent that takes in untrusted content (web pages, files, inbound email, chat, support tickets, form submissions, or API responses) also holds access to sensitive data and has any outbound channel, such as browsing, API calls, messages, or tool calls that carry data in URLs. Instructions injected through the content can then direct the agent to send data out through a legitimate channel, for example by fetching an attacker's URL with data in it, by replying or forwarding to an attacker's address, or by posting to a shared channel. Each capability may be individually controlled; the exposure comes from their combination, and the way in and the way out can be the same channel. As a result, confidential data can leave the organisation without any single control being bypassed, as demonstrated by EchoLeak, where a single crafted email led Microsoft 365 Copilot to send internal data to an attacker, and ForcedLeak, where instructions in a web-form submission led Salesforce Agentforce to exfiltrate CRM records.

risks.statement: Compromise through the tool, skill, and dependency supply chain
risks.description: This risk arises when the tools, MCP servers, agent "skills" or plug-ins, prompt templates, and software packages an agent relies on are obtained through registries, marketplaces, package managers, or update channels that an attacker can seed, tamper with, or silently change after approval (the "rug pull"). controls.statement: Treat all tool metadata and outputs as untrusted input requiring validation
controls.recommendations: Tool metadata (descriptions, parameter names, schema definitions) can contain prompt injection attacks that manipulate agent behaviour even without tool invocation, whilst tool outputs may contain malicious content designed to compromise downstream systems. Validate and sanitise all tool metadata before exposing it to the LLM, treating tool descriptions with the same scrutiny as external user input and implementing content filtering to detect embedded instructions or adversarial prompts. Apply strict schema validation to tool outputs and sanitise responses before using them in prompts, displaying them to users, or passing them to other systems. Implement monitoring and logging of tool metadata and outputs to enable detection of injection attempts and post-incident analysis of compromised tool behaviour.

risks.statement: Escape from evaluation or sandbox containment onto live systems
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent that can execute code, operating in what is intended to be a contained setting — an evaluation, a red-team exercise, or a sandboxed task — reaches real systems because containment is incomplete: network egress is open, real credentials or accounts are present, or the objective can be pursued more easily outside the boundary. As a result, activity meant to be harmless produces real-world security incidents.

controls.statement: Grant agents only the minimum permissions required for their designated tasks

risks.statement: Deceptive behaviour toward overseers

Establish comprehensive pre-deployment testing that evaluates agent safety across domain-specific stress scenarios, including adversarial inputs designed to trigger unsafe behaviour, edge cases that challenge safety boundaries, and failure modes that test resilience under degraded conditions. Document test results, identified vulnerabilities, and implemented mitigations for future reference and regular review. Repeat the exercise on a fixed cadence and whenever the model, tools, or capabilities change - attacks evolve faster than deployments. Use established agent security and safety benchmarks (for example AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, and AgentHarm) as a baseline and add scenarios drawn from your own incidents and from published ones.

risks.statement: Unsanctioned coordination between agents
risks.description: This risk arises when agents in a multi-agent system coordinate through channels or in ways that no operator sanctioned — sharing credentials, leaving each other messages in shared stores, using side channels, or dividing up a task so that each agent's actions look acceptable while the combined outcome is not. controls.statement: Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
controls.recommendations: Unstructured or inadequately validated inter-agent messages create vulnerability to injection attacks, misinterpretation, and parsing errors that could compromise agent behaviour or cascade through multi-agent systems. Define explicit message schemas using formal specification languages (e.g., JSON Schema, Protobuf, OpenAPI) that specify required fields, data types, validation rules, and permitted value ranges for all agent-to-agent communications. Implement strict input validation that verifies all incoming messages conform to expected schemas, checking field presence, data types, value ranges, and structural integrity before processing message content. Reject messages that are incomplete, contain unexpected fields, violate type constraints, or include suspicious patterns, returning explicit error responses to the sending agent and logging validation failures to enable detection of compromised or malfunctioning agents.

Reject unauthenticated requests immediately and log authentication failures to detect potential impersonation attempts or compromised agents attempting to bypass security controls. Both the A2A Protocol and LangGraph provide native support for cryptographic agent authentication through mTLS, OAuth 2.0, and JWT-based identity verification.

risks.statement: Automation bias and erosion of human oversight
risks.description: This risk arises when human approval steps stop providing meaningful review: overseers approve by default under volume (one large deployment measured users approving around 93% of permission prompts), lack the context or expertise to evaluate what the agent proposes, or use interfaces designed for speed rather than scrutiny. Controls that assume a considered human decision then give false assurance, and adversaries can exploit the trust users place in fluent, confident agents. As a result, high-impact actions proceed with nominal rather than actual oversight.

controls.statement: Require explicit human confirmation before executing high-impact or irreversible tool actions
controls.recommendations: Agents may incorrectly select or misuse high-impact tools, leading to irreversible damage such as data deletion, unauthorised financial transactions, or unintended system modifications. Implement mandatory human-in-the-loop approval workflows for tools that perform high-impact or irreversible actions, including sending external communications, executing financial transactions, deleting or modifying critical data, and making privileged configuration changes. Configure approval interfaces to clearly display the tool being invoked, the parameters being passed, and the expected outcome, enabling informed human decision-making. Ensure approval mechanisms cannot be bypassed by agents and maintain audit logs of all approval decisions, including who approved what action and when. Approval steps decay under volume: in one large deployment users approved about 93% of permission prompts. Pair this control with CTRL-0094 - measure approval and override rates, route routine actions to automated screening, and reserve human approval for genuinely uncertain or high-impact actions so that the approvals that remain are real decisions.
controls.evidence: The tool registry marking each irreversible tool as confirmation-required, and the audit log recording who confirmed which tool call, with parameters and time.
controls.test: Invoke a tool marked irreversible through the tool layer without a confirmation record and confirm the call is refused and logged.

risks.description: This risk arises when tasks are delegated to, or transactions conducted with, agents provided or operated by external parties — SaaS agents, partner agents reached through protocols such as A2A — whose instructions, tools, data handling, and updates are outside the organisation's control. controls.statement: Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
controls.recommendations: Unstructured or inadequately validated inter-agent messages create vulnerability to injection attacks, misinterpretation, and parsing errors that could compromise agent behaviour or cascade through multi-agent systems. Define explicit message schemas using formal specification languages (e.g., JSON Schema, Protobuf, OpenAPI) that specify required fields, data types, validation rules, and permitted value ranges for all agent-to-agent communications. Implement strict input validation that verifies all incoming messages conform to expected schemas, checking field presence, data types, value ranges, and structural integrity before processing message content. Reject messages that are incomplete, contain unexpected fields, violate type constraints, or include suspicious patterns, returning explicit error responses to the sending agent and logging validation failures to enable detection of compromised or malfunctioning agents.

controls.statement: Ensure all inter-agent communications are encrypted in transit and prohibit plaintext channels
controls.recommendations: Unencrypted inter-agent communications expose sensitive data, credentials, and operational context to network-based attackers through eavesdropping or man-in-the-middle attacks. Ensure all agent-to-agent network communications use transport-layer encryption (minimum TLS 1.2, preferably TLS 1.3), including internal traffic within trusted network boundaries, as internal networks are increasingly targeted by sophisticated attackers. For protocol-based frameworks (e.g., A2A Protocol), verify that TLS is enabled by default; for application frameworks (e.g., LangGraph, CrewAI), configure deployment infrastructure to enforce HTTPS endpoints for all remote agent APIs. Configure agents to reject plaintext connections and verify certificates to prevent downgrade attacks or rogue agent impersonation, and regularly audit network traffic to detect agents attempting unencrypted communication.

controls.statement: Require all agents to authenticate with verifiable, cryptographically signed identities before processing requests
controls.recommendations: Without strong agent authentication, attackers can impersonate legitimate agents to gain unauthorised access, inject malicious commands, or exfiltrate sensitive data from multi-agent systems. risks.statement: Insecure default configuration of agent frameworks and runtimes
risks.description: This risk arises when the frameworks and runtimes an agent is built on ship with insecure defaults — authentication disabled, services listening on all interfaces, permissive origin checks on local control channels, unsafe deserialisation of persisted state, or default credentials — and deployers inherit them unchanged. As a result, any reachable attacker can drive the agent and use the credentials and tools it holds, as shown by a one-click remote-code-execution flaw in a widely installed open-source agent and a chain of deserialisation flaws in agent orchestration frameworks.

controls.statement: Use only tool servers and APIs, including MCP servers, that implement robust authentication mechanisms in production environments
controls.recommendations: Weak or misconfigured authorisation on the servers and APIs that an agent's tools call can lead to unauthorised access, token theft, or privilege escalation that compromises connected systems. Before deployment, verify that every remote tool endpoint authenticates its caller with a standard mechanism (for example OAuth 2.1, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, or mutually authenticated TLS) and enforces per-client scopes, and reject endpoints that rely on hard-coded credentials, unscoped shared keys, or deprecated authentication methods; test the authorisation flows in a development environment to confirm them. For MCP servers, also verify per-client consent flows and redirect URI validation to prevent authorisation bypasses, and reject servers with insufficient session management. As of the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, verify additionally that the server implements RFC 9207 issuer identification (so a client can detect a substituted authorization server) and Client ID Metadata Documents in place of dynamic client registration, and prefer servers that support the Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension so that access is governed by your identity provider rather than by per-user ad-hoc consent. Treat servers still built on the pre-2026 stateful session model as needing review before production use.
controls.evidence: The tool endpoint inventory recording each remote server's authentication mechanism and per-client scopes, with the integration review that exercised its authorisation flow.
controls.test: Call each production tool endpoint with no credential and with a credential scoped for a different client, and confirm both are refused.

risks.statement: Actions beyond the agent's tools through code execution and reachable credentials
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent that can run code can also read files, environment variables, or data stores that hold credentials, tokens, or keys, so the code it writes can act with whatever those credentials allow instead of only through the tools it was given. Approval steps, allowlists, and rate limits placed on the agent's tools then do not constrain it, because the code calls the database, cloud API, or deployment platform directly. As a result, a misjudgement or an injected instruction can cause destructive or unauthorised actions far outside the agent's intended scope, as when a coding agent used a broadly scoped infrastructure token to delete a company's production database and the backups stored with it, and when a coding agent deleted a live production database during a code freeze.

controls.statement: Grant agents only the minimum permissions required for their designated tasks
controls.recommendations: Excessive permissions enable compromised or malfunctioning agents to access sensitive resources, modify critical data, or perform actions beyond their intended scope, amplifying the impact of security breaches. Apply the principle of least privilege by defining granular permission sets for each agent based on its specific role and required operations, avoiding blanket administrative access or broad permission grants. Review agent permissions regularly to ensure they remain aligned with current responsibilities, revoking unnecessary access as agent roles evolve.
controls.evidence: Each agent's IAM policy and tool permission manifest, with every permission tied to a named task, and the latest access review record.
controls.test: Using the agent's credentials, attempt an operation outside its role, such as reading another system's data store, and confirm it is denied.

controls.statement: Conduct safety verification with domain-relevant stress tests and adversarial scenarios before deployment and on a regular cadence afterwards
controls.recommendations: Deploying agents without rigorous safety testing risks exposing users to harmful behaviours, security vulnerabilities, or compliance violations that only emerge under adversarial or edge-case conditions. Design test scenarios based on known risks in your domain (e.g., financial fraud attempts for banking agents, medical misinformation for healthcare agents, data exfiltration for enterprise assistants) and establish clear pass/fail criteria that must be met before deployment. Repeat the exercise on a fixed cadence and whenever the model, tools, or capabilities change - attacks evolve faster than deployments. risks.description: This risk arises when an agent loads instructions, rules, settings, hooks, skills, or tool configuration from files that someone other than its operator can write: a rules file in a cloned repository, an instruction file in a downloads folder, a project-level settings file, or a tool configuration that the agent itself can edit. These files are read automatically, often before any trust prompt, and what they contain is treated as the operator's own instructions or runs as commands. As a result, anyone who can place or change such a file can direct the agent or run code on the machine it works on, and the change persists across sessions, as when malicious packages planted hidden instructions in coding assistants' instruction files, a cloned repository's settings took effect before the user was asked to trust it, and a crafted chat message led a coding agent to rewrite its own tool configuration.

controls.statement: Keep untrusted inputs out of system instructions, and enclose any untrusted content given to the model in delimiters marked as data
controls.recommendations: Prompt injection attacks exploit LLMs' inability to distinguish between instructions and data, allowing malicious users to embed commands within input that override intended behaviour. Do not interpolate user input, retrieved content, or tool outputs into the system prompt or other instruction templates; fix the system prompt at build time and pass untrusted content to the model in the user or tool turns, where it carries less authority. Where untrusted content must be quoted, enclose it within clearly marked boundaries (e.g., XML tags or special markers) that are unlikely to appear naturally in the input, and instruct the LLM to treat delimited content as data rather than instructions. Neither measure is a complete defence, because the model can still follow instructions in untrusted content, so combine them with controls that do not depend on the model's compliance, such as a deterministic policy layer (CTRL-0090) and least privilege (CTRL-0029).

controls.statement: Require verified provenance for tools, skills, and dependencies, and re-verify them on every update

controls.statement: Enforce data-flow and capability policies at runtime with a deterministic policy layer that separates untrusted content from privileged actions
controls.recommendations: Classifier-based injection guardrails are probabilistic and do not close the attack. Complement them with an architectural boundary in which untrusted content never directly drives privileged actions - for example a privileged planner that never sees raw untrusted data working with a quarantined model that extracts values from it (the dual-LLM pattern), capability or information-flow labels that follow data through the system, and a policy engine that checks each tool call against what the data it depends on is allowed to do. Published designs such as CaMeL, Progent, and related reference monitors largely eliminate injection success on agent benchmarks; adopt one, or an equivalent policy layer in your framework, for systems that combine untrusted content with sensitive data or consequential actions.

risks.statement: Agent credentials that are over-broad, long-lived, or outlive their use
risks.description: This risk arises when the identities and credentials that agents use are broader than the task needs, do not expire, are stored where other software can read them, or stay valid after the agent, the integration, or the vendor relationship has ended. Agents, and the platforms and vendors that act for them, accumulate tokens for many systems, and a single theft then opens all of them. As a result, a compromise of an agent, of a developer's machine, or of an agent vendor gives an attacker standing access to the organisation's systems, as when stolen tokens belonging to a sales chat agent were used to pull data from hundreds of its customers' environments, a breach at an agent-integration platform exposed more than ten thousand credentials held for customers' agents, and a software release was hijacked through an agent-platform key that had never been revoked.

controls.statement: Limit token scopes to the minimum privileges required and avoid broad or wildcard scopes
controls.recommendations: Overly broad token scopes enable compromised or malicious actors to access resources beyond what is necessary for legitimate operations, amplifying the impact of security breaches. Define granular, task-specific scopes for each MCP server integration and request only the minimum permissions required for the intended functionality (e.g., "read:inventory" rather than "admin:*"). Review and document the justification for each requested scope during integration, and reject MCP servers that require unnecessarily broad permissions or fail to support fine-grained scope definitions. Periodically audit active token scopes to identify and revoke excessive permissions that may have accumulated over time.
controls.evidence: The OAuth client configuration listing each scope requested per tool integration with its justification, containing no wildcard or administrator scope.
controls.test: Decode a token issued to the agent in production, confirm its scopes match the configured list, then call an out-of-scope operation and confirm refusal.

controls.statement: Assign each agent a unique, verifiable identity with no shared credentials
controls.recommendations: Shared credentials prevent accurate attribution of agent actions, making it impossible to identify which agent performed unauthorised activities or to revoke access for compromised agents without affecting legitimate ones. Assign each agent instance a unique identity (e.g., service account, API key, certificate) that can be independently tracked, audited, and revoked without impacting other agents. Prohibit credential sharing between agents even when they perform similar functions, as unique identities enable granular access control and forensic analysis of agent behaviour. Emerging agentic IAM platforms, such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, can help to provide purpose-built identity management for AI agents. Concrete mechanisms now exist: SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identities with short rotation for agents and MCP servers, Microsoft Entra Agent ID (assigned to all new Copilot Studio agents since July 2026), and the IETF drafts for OAuth on-behalf-of delegation and transaction tokens that carry separate actor (agent) and principal (initiating human) claims; A2A v1.0 signed agent cards provide the equivalent for agent-to-agent interactions. Prefer identities that keep the delegating human visible in every token so that actions remain attributable.
controls.evidence: The identity provider's list of agent service accounts or workload identities, showing one per agent instance and no key shared between two.
controls.test: Revoke one agent's credential and confirm only that agent loses access, and that the audit log attributes its earlier actions to it alone.

risks.statement: Dependence on a model provider
risks.description: This risk arises when an agentic system depends on a model that another party hosts, and that party withdraws it, changes it, limits access to it, or suffers an outage. A model can be retired at short notice, updated in ways that change how it calls tools or follows instructions, degraded by a fault on the provider's side that goes unannounced for weeks, or made unavailable by a commercial or regulatory decision. As a result, an agent may stop working, or may keep working while behaving differently from the system that was evaluated and approved, as when infrastructure faults at a provider silently degraded model output for weeks, a provider disabled two models for all customers following an export-control directive, and a regional degradation at a provider caused cascading failures in a customer-service agent product.

controls.statement: Conduct structured evaluation of multiple LLMs for instruction-following, performance, and safety before deployment
controls.recommendations: Deploying an LLM without comparative evaluation risks selecting a model poorly suited to your use case, potentially resulting in safety issues, poor performance, or misaligned behaviour. Define evaluation criteria aligned with your application requirements (e.g., accuracy on domain-specific tasks, refusal of unsafe requests, consistency of outputs) and benchmark multiple candidate models against these criteria using representative test scenarios. Use both automated metrics and human evaluation to assess instruction-following quality, safety boundaries, and failure modes. Document evaluation results to support model selection decisions and establish baseline performance expectations for ongoing monitoring.
controls.evidence: The evaluation report scoring at least two candidate models on one test set for instruction-following, task performance and safety, with the selection decision.
controls.test: Re-run the stored evaluation set against the deployed model version and confirm its scores fall within the tolerance recorded in the report.

controls.statement: Conduct safety verification with domain-relevant stress tests and adversarial scenarios before deployment and on a regular cadence afterwards
controls.recommendations: Deploying agents without rigorous safety testing risks exposing users to harmful behaviours, security vulnerabilities, or compliance violations that only emerge under adversarial or edge-case conditions. Establish comprehensive pre-deployment testing that evaluates agent safety across domain-specific stress scenarios, including adversarial inputs designed to trigger unsafe behaviour, edge cases that challenge safety boundaries, and failure modes that test resilience under degraded conditions. Design test scenarios based on known risks in your domain (e.g., financial fraud attempts for banking agents, medical misinformation for healthcare agents, data exfiltration for enterprise assistants) and establish clear pass/fail criteria that must be met before deployment. Document test results, identified vulnerabilities, and implemented mitigations for future reference and regular review. Repeat the exercise on a fixed cadence and whenever the model, tools, or capabilities change - attacks evolve faster than deployments. Use established agent security and safety benchmarks (for example AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, and AgentHarm) as a baseline and add scenarios drawn from your own incidents and from published ones.

controls.test: Run AgentDojo, AgentHarm and the system's own domain scenarios against the release candidate and confirm the results meet the recorded pass criteria.

risks.statement: Agent alters or disables the oversight placed on it
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent is able to change the logs, monitors, permissions, approval settings, or configuration that are meant to constrain it, and does so in pursuit of its task or at the direction of injected content. controls.statement: Centralise observability data collection in a unified backend system

Configure agents to emit structured telemetry with consistent identifiers (agent IDs, session IDs, request IDs) that enable tracing requests across agent boundaries and reconstructing complete workflow execution paths.

risks.statement: Authority passing between agents without a check
risks.description: This risk arises when one agent treats a request or a message from another agent as authorisation to act, without checking that the person on whose behalf the first agent is working is entitled to that action. A low-privilege agent can then ask a higher-privilege agent to do what it cannot do itself, and an attacker who can influence any agent in the chain, or who can write somewhere that an agent reads, borrows the privileges of the most powerful one. As a result, the access controls set for each agent are bypassed by the path between them, as when an injected low-privilege agent recruited a higher-privilege agent through agent discovery to copy records it could not read itself, a prompt posted by one company's agent was executed as a transfer instruction by another company's agent, and a public triage agent was led to invoke a workflow reserved for maintainers.

controls.statement: Define formal schemas for inter-agent messages and validate all messages against these schemas before processing
controls.recommendations: Unstructured or inadequately validated inter-agent messages create vulnerability to injection attacks, misinterpretation, and parsing errors that could compromise agent behaviour or cascade through multi-agent systems. Define explicit message schemas using formal specification languages (e.g., JSON Schema, Protobuf, OpenAPI) that specify required fields, data types, validation rules, and permitted value ranges for all agent-to-agent communications. Implement strict input validation that verifies all incoming messages conform to expected schemas, checking field presence, data types, value ranges, and structural integrity before processing message content. Reject messages that are incomplete, contain unexpected fields, violate type constraints, or include suspicious patterns, returning explicit error responses to the sending agent and logging validation failures to enable detection of compromised or malfunctioning agents.
controls.evidence: The inter-agent message schemas in version control and the validator invoked at each agent's message entry point.
controls.test: Send an agent a message with a missing required field and an undeclared extra field and confirm it returns an error and logs a validation failure.

controls.statement: Require all agents to authenticate with verifiable, cryptographically signed identities before processing requests

Configure the authentication system to validate that credentials are properly signed by a trusted authority, have not expired, and belong to the claimed agent identity. Reject unauthenticated requests immediately and log authentication failures to detect potential impersonation attempts or compromised agents attempting to bypass security controls. Both the A2A Protocol and LangGraph provide native support for cryptographic agent authentication through mTLS, OAuth 2.0, and JWT-based identity verification.

Do not let agents discover and call each other freely: list which agents may call which, and for which actions. Treat a message from another organisation's agent as untrusted input, and require a human or an out-of-band confirmation before acting on it where the action is consequential.

risks.statement: Harm from a connected tool server or agent to the system that connects to it
risks.description: This risk arises when a tool server or agent that another party builds or operates attacks the system that connects to it, or fails in a way that damages it. The connection itself is the route: a malicious server can abuse the protocol's authorisation or discovery steps to run commands on the connecting machine, obtain credentials meant for other services, or pose as a trusted server, and a faulty shared server can deliver one client's results to another. RISK-006 covers a connected party misleading the agent through what it says about itself; this risk covers harm that needs no cooperation from the model at all. As a result, connecting to a server can compromise the host, its credentials, or other users' data, as when a malicious tool server could run commands on any machine that connected to it through a widely used client, and a race condition in a protocol library sent tool results to the wrong client.

controls.statement: Use only tool servers and APIs, including MCP servers, that implement robust authentication mechanisms in production environments
controls.recommendations: Weak or misconfigured authorisation on the servers and APIs that an agent's tools call can lead to unauthorised access, token theft, or privilege escalation that compromises connected systems. Before deployment, verify that every remote tool endpoint authenticates its caller with a standard mechanism (for example OAuth 2.1, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, or mutually authenticated TLS) and enforces per-client scopes, and reject endpoints that rely on hard-coded credentials, unscoped shared keys, or deprecated authentication methods; test the authorisation flows in a development environment to confirm them. For MCP servers, also verify per-client consent flows and redirect URI validation to prevent authorisation bypasses, and reject servers with insufficient session management. As of the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, verify additionally that the server implements RFC 9207 issuer identification (so a client can detect a substituted authorization server) and Client ID Metadata Documents in place of dynamic client registration, and prefer servers that support the Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension so that access is governed by your identity provider rather than by per-user ad-hoc consent. Treat servers still built on the pre-2026 stateful session model as needing review before production use.
controls.evidence: The tool endpoint inventory recording each remote server's authentication mechanism and per-client scopes, with the integration review that exercised its authorisation flow.
controls.test: Call each production tool endpoint with no credential and with a credential scoped for a different client, and confirm both are refused.

controls.statement: Use only MCP servers that validate credentials on every inbound request
controls.recommendations: Relying on session state or connection-based authentication without per-request validation creates vulnerability to session hijacking, token replay attacks, and unauthorised access after initial authentication. Verify that MCP servers implement stateless authentication by validating credentials (e.g., OAuth tokens, API keys) on every single request rather than caching authorisation decisions based on connection or session state. Test this behaviour by monitoring whether the server accepts requests with expired, revoked, or missing credentials after an initial successful authentication. Ensure the server responds with appropriate HTTP 401 errors when credentials are invalid, expired, or absent, forcing re-authentication rather than relying on stale authorisation state. The 2026-07-28 specification removes long-lived stateful sessions from the protocol core, making per-request validation the expected behaviour; treat a server whose authorization depends on session state as non-compliant.
controls.evidence: The MCP server assessment record containing captured responses to requests sent with expired, revoked and missing tokens after an initial successful login.
controls.test: Authenticate to the MCP server, revoke the token, send another request on the same connection and confirm it returns HTTP 401.

controls.statement: Use only MCP servers that validate token provenance and prohibit unauthorised token passthrough
controls.recommendations: Token passthrough is an anti-pattern where MCP servers accept tokens from clients without validating they were properly issued to the server, enabling malicious actors to use the server as a proxy for data exfiltration with stolen tokens. Verify that MCP servers validate the provenance of all tokens they receive, ensuring tokens are intended for that specific server by checking audience claims and preventing tokens from being blindly forwarded to third-party services. Reject MCP servers that implement token passthrough patterns, as they compromise incident investigation, access controls, and auditing capabilities by obscuring the true source of requests. Since the 2026-07-28 specification, servers must validate the issuer of tokens they receive (RFC 9207) as well as the audience; reject servers that accept tokens from unexpected issuers or forward tokens they cannot prove were issued to them.
controls.evidence: The MCP server assessment record showing audience and issuer validation tested, alongside the server's token-validation settings.

controls.recommendations: Treat tools, MCP servers, agent skills or plug-ins, prompt templates, and packages as supply chain artefacts. controls.statement: Harden agent frameworks and runtimes before exposing them, and patch framework vulnerabilities promptly
controls.recommendations: Do not run an agent framework with its defaults on any reachable network. Before exposure, enable authentication on every control interface, bind local services to loopback rather than all interfaces, validate origins on WebSocket and browser-facing endpoints, disable or replace unsafe deserialisation of persisted state and checkpoints, remove default credentials, and run the agent as an unprivileged user. Track security advisories for the frameworks and SDKs in use and treat agent-framework vulnerabilities as high priority for patching, because an agent runtime typically holds the credentials of everything it can act on. Include these checks in the deployment baseline so that a new agent cannot go live unhardened.
