risks.statement: Instructions or approvals forged in the principal's name
risks.description: This risk arises when something other than the principal can supply what the agent treats as the principal's own instruction or approval. A link can open the agent with a prompt already filled in and submitted, another program or browser extension on the same machine can drive the agent's interface or click its approval prompts, a command-line flag can start the agent with its permission checks turned off, and a compromised operator console can queue instructions as if they came from the operator. The register's injection risks concern content that the agent reads; here the attacker speaks with the user's voice. As a result, the agent carries out an attacker's request with the user's full authority, and its approval steps are satisfied without a person, as when a link with a pre-filled prompt made an assistant send the user's data to an attacker, malicious packages invoked developers' locally installed coding agents with their safety checks disabled, and a trading agent sent funds to an attacker who had queued prompts through its operator dashboard.

controls.statement: Require explicit human confirmation before executing high-impact or irreversible tool actions
controls.recommendations: Agents may incorrectly select or misuse high-impact tools, leading to irreversible damage such as data deletion, unauthorised financial transactions, or unintended system modifications. Implement mandatory human-in-the-loop approval workflows for tools that perform high-impact or irreversible actions, including sending external communications, executing financial transactions, deleting or modifying critical data, and making privileged configuration changes. Configure approval interfaces to clearly display the tool being invoked, the parameters being passed, and the expected outcome, enabling informed human decision-making. Ensure approval mechanisms cannot be bypassed by agents and maintain audit logs of all approval decisions, including who approved what action and when. Approval steps decay under volume: in one large deployment users approved about 93% of permission prompts. Pair this control with CTRL-0094 - measure approval and override rates, route routine actions to automated screening, and reserve human approval for genuinely uncertain or high-impact actions so that the approvals that remain are real decisions.
controls.evidence: The tool registry marking each irreversible tool as confirmation-required, and the audit log recording who confirmed which tool call, with parameters and time.
controls.test: Invoke a tool marked irreversible through the tool layer without a confirmation record and confirm the call is refused and logged.

risks.statement: Personal data collected, kept, or passed on beyond what the task needs
risks.description: This risk arises when an agent gathers, keeps, or passes on more personal data than its task requires. It may index a whole mailbox or drive to answer one question and keep the index afterwards, record people who have not agreed to it, place personal details in a search query or in an API call to another company, or upload local files to a hosted service by default. No one need attack the agent for this to happen, and each step can look like ordinary tool use. As a result, personal data is held without a purpose, reaches third parties that have no right to it, or is published, in breach of data protection obligations, as when a coding assistant uploaded users' whole local repositories to a cloud service by default, a personal assistant kept indexed email in place after it was no longer needed, and agents posted users' images to public image-hosting sites.

controls.statement: Implement output guardrails to detect and redact personally identifiable information
controls.recommendations: Agents may reproduce personally identifiable information from training data, memory, or prior interactions in their outputs, violating privacy obligations, exposing individuals to harm, or breaching data protection requirements such as GDPR or PDPA. Deploy output guardrails that scan all agent-generated content for PII categories including names, email addresses, phone numbers, identification numbers, financial account details, and other sensitive personal data before delivery to users. Use PII detection tools, pattern matching, or named entity recognition models to identify and redact or block outputs containing PII. Configure appropriate handling based on context — some PII may be acceptable if it belongs to the current user, whilst PII belonging to other individuals should be strictly prevented from disclosure.
controls.evidence: The output filter configuration listing the personal data types detected and the action for each, with redaction counts in the guardrail log.
controls.test: Prompt the agent to repeat a seeded record holding another person's identity number, phone number and email and confirm all three arrive redacted.

risks.statement: Use of the agent by its own principal against others
risks.description: This risk arises when the person or organisation that an agent works for directs it to act against others, or deploys it in a way that disregards them. A user may have it gather and compile personal information about people, build material for fraud, or act on another party's service in breach of that party's terms while disguised as a human; an operator may release an agent that transacts with businesses that never agreed to it. The agent does what it is told, so controls aimed at manipulation and error do not apply, and safeguards that judge each step in isolation can be defeated by spreading a harmful aim across routine steps. As a result, the organisation that provides or operates the agent may be answerable for harassment, privacy violations, fraud, or unauthorised access carried out through it, as when an agent compiled lists of people in vulnerable groups on request, an app-building agent produced and hosted complete phishing pages, and a shopping agent was alleged to have entered customer accounts on a retailer's site while presenting itself as a human user.

controls.statement: Implement automated alerts when agent behaviour drifts from predefined thresholds
controls.recommendations: Behavioural drift may indicate model degradation, adversarial manipulation, or emergent unsafe patterns that require immediate investigation. Define baseline metrics for expected agent behaviour (e.g., tool usage patterns, response times, error rates, decision distributions) and establish acceptable variance thresholds based on your risk tolerance. Implement monitoring systems that continuously track these metrics and trigger alerts when deviations exceed thresholds, enabling rapid response to anomalies. Configure alerts to include sufficient diagnostic context (timestamp, affected sessions, deviation magnitude) and establish clear escalation procedures for investigating and remediating drift incidents.
controls.evidence: The alert rules in the monitoring system, each naming a behavioural metric, its baseline, its threshold and the escalation route.
controls.test: Replay a staging session with ten times the baseline tool-call rate and confirm an alert fires naming the session and the size of the deviation.

controls.statement: Conduct safety verification with domain-relevant stress tests and adversarial scenarios before deployment and on a regular cadence afterwards
controls.recommendations: Deploying agents without rigorous safety testing risks exposing users to harmful behaviours, security vulnerabilities, or compliance violations that only emerge under adversarial or edge-case conditions. Establish comprehensive pre-deployment testing that evaluates agent safety across domain-specific stress scenarios, including adversarial inputs designed to trigger unsafe behaviour, edge cases that challenge safety boundaries, and failure modes that test resilience under degraded conditions. Design test scenarios based on known risks in your domain (e.g., financial fraud attempts for banking agents, medical misinformation for healthcare agents, data exfiltration for enterprise assistants) and establish clear pass/fail criteria that must be met before deployment. Document test results, identified vulnerabilities, and implemented mitigations for future reference and regular review. Repeat the exercise on a fixed cadence and whenever the model, tools, or capabilities change - attacks evolve faster than deployments. Use established agent security and safety benchmarks (for example AgentDojo, Agent Security Bench, and AgentHarm) as a baseline and add scenarios drawn from your own incidents and from published ones.
controls.evidence: The dated safety test report listing domain stress scenarios, pass criteria, results, findings and mitigations, with a rerun after each model or tool change.
controls.test: Run AgentDojo, AgentHarm and the system's own domain scenarios against the release candidate and confirm the results meet the recorded pass criteria.

elements.name: LLM
elements.description: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on massive text data to learn statistical patterns of language, enabling it to understand, generate, and reason over natural language inputs. It is the core reasoning engine that processes instructions, interprets user inputs, and generates contextually appropriate responses by leveraging its trained language understanding and generation capabilities. There are a large variety of LLMs to choose from, with different sizes, capabilities, and architectures, from large closed-source model families such as OpenAI's GPT, Anthropic's Claude, and Google's Gemini, to open-weights families such as Llama, Qwen, and Mistral, which include small models that can run on local hardware.

elements.name: Instructions
elements.description: Instructions are structured inputs provided to an LLM that define the task, constraints, and context, guiding how the model interprets inputs and generates outputs. They guide the LLM's decision process by conditioning prompts and tool use with objectives, policies, and guardrails. Forms include system prompts, policies, schemas, and rubrics, varying by framework and enforcement strictness.

elements.name: Tools
elements.description: Tools are external functions, APIs, or resources attached to an LLM that extend its capabilities beyond text generation, enabling it to retrieve information, execute actions, and affect external systems (e.g., search, code execution, database queries, or file manipulation), typically through structured interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that constrain invocation, inputs, permissions, and outputs for agentic control and safety.

elements.name: Memory
elements.description: Memory is a persistent or semi-persistent data store attached to an LLM that retains information across interactions—such as conversation history, user preferences, task state, and retrieved knowledge—enabling continuity, long-horizon reasoning, and personalization in agentic workflows. Memory may be implemented through mechanisms such as context windows, vector databases, episodic logs, or external state stores, each offering different trade-offs in latency, fidelity, and persistence. Every agent has working memory, the context it carries within a task; a system has persistent memory when it keeps information beyond a single session or shares it across users or tasks.
elements.present_when: The system keeps information beyond a single session, or shares it across users or tasks.

elements.name: Protocols
elements.description: Protocols are the standard interfaces through which an agentic system connects to tools, services, and agents that another party builds or operates, such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool servers and agent-to-agent protocols such as A2A. A protocol governs how the other party is discovered, how it is identified and authenticated, what it declares about itself to the agent (tool descriptions, capability lists, agent cards), and how requests and results pass between the two. A system has this component when it makes at least one such connection, in either direction: its agents reach another party's tool server or agent, or another party's agents reach it. A function or API wrapper that the system's own team writes is a tool, not a protocol connection, because the team controls the description the agent sees.
elements.present_when: At least one tool server or agent that another party builds or operates is connected to the system through an agent protocol such as MCP or A2A, in either direction.

elements.name: Agentic Architecture
elements.description: The agentic architecture defines how an agentic system's control flow is structured: the loop through which a single agent plans, acts, and observes, and, where there are several agents, how they are structured, interconnected, and coordinated to collectively perform tasks that exceed the capabilities of a single agent. This includes orchestration patterns such as hierarchical delegation, parallel agent execution, sequential handoffs between specialised agents, shared or centralized planning components, and the communication protocols that govern information exchange and coordination across the system. Risks specific to multiple agents apply only to systems with the Agent Delegation capability.

elements.name: Roles and Access Controls
elements.description: Roles and access controls define and enforce differentiated roles, permissions, and scopes of authority across agents and system components, specifying what actions each agent is allowed to perform and which resources it may access. This includes assigning functional roles to agents, configuring tool- and data-level permissions, scoping credentials or identities, and enforcing access policies that govern interactions with files, systems, services, or other agents.

elements.name: Monitoring and Traceability
elements.description: Monitoring and traceability provide systematic visibility into agent behaviour, interactions, and decision pathways by recording, observing, and correlating agent actions and system events over time. This includes logging agent inputs and outputs, tracking tool invocations and state changes, capturing decision traces or execution paths, and surfacing telemetry or audit records that support analysis and review of system behaviour.

elements.name: Planning and Goal Management
elements.description: The capability to develop detailed, step-by-step, and executable plans with specific tasks in response to broad instructions. This includes prioritizing activities based on importance and dependencies between tasks, monitoring how well its plan is working, and adjusting when circumstances change or obstacles arise.

elements.name: Agent Delegation
elements.description: The capability to assign subtasks to other agents and coordinate their activities to achieve broader goals. This includes identifying which components are best suited for specific tasks, issuing clear instructions, managing inter-agent dependencies, and monitoring performance or failures. A system has this capability whenever more than one agent works on a task, whether an agent decides the hand-offs or they are fixed in the workflow, and whether the other agents belong to the same system or are operated by another party, including agents it transacts with as counterparties.

elements.name: Tool Use
elements.description: The capability to evaluate available options and choose the best tool for specific subtasks, based on the capabilities and limitations of different tools and matching them appropriately to the tasks. This includes selecting between search, computation, code execution, or domain-specific APIs, determining when tool invocation is necessary, and sequencing or combining multiple tools to complete complex tasks effectively.

elements.name: Multimodal Understanding and Generation
elements.description: The capability to communicate with human users across multiple modalities, including natural language conversation (explaining topics, generating documents, interactive discussions) and multimodal understanding/generation (processing and creating image, audio, or video content such as visual analysis, speech transcription, or multimedia creation).

elements.name: Official Communication
elements.description: The capability to compose, finalise, and dispatch authoritative communications that formally and legally represent an organization to external parties (e.g. customers, partners, regulators, courts, or media) via approved channels and formats, thereby creating potential legal, regulatory, or reputational obligations. This includes sending legally binding correspondence, publishing official statements or press releases, and responding to external inquiries using the organisation's identity. A system has this capability whether a person sends what the agent drafts, approves each message before it goes, or lets the agent send by itself; that difference is recorded as the capability's authority.

elements.name: Business Transactions
elements.description: The capability to initiate, authorise, and execute binding business transactions with external parties - such as payments, purchases, reservations, or service commitments - resulting in real financial, contractual, or operational obligations for the organization. This includes processing payments or refunds, placing orders or subscriptions, booking services or reservations, and accepting or triggering contractual commitments on behalf of the organization. A system has this capability whether a person completes the transactions the agent prepares, approves each one, or lets the agent transact by itself within limits set in advance; that difference is recorded as the capability's authority.

elements.name: Internet and Search Access
elements.description: The capability to autonomously access, browse, search, and retrieve information from the Internet to augment the LLM's static training knowledge with external and up-to-date sources in support of task execution and response generation. This includes issuing search queries, following and parsing web pages, extracting relevant facts or documents, and aggregating information from multiple online sources.

elements.name: Computer Use
elements.description: The capability to directly operate a computer’s graphical user interface on behalf of the user, enabling the agent to navigate applications and execute tasks through mouse, keyboard, and window-based interactions. This includes moving the cursor, clicking buttons, entering text, using keyboard shortcuts, switching between windows and applications, and navigating files and menus within the operating system environment.

elements.name: Other Programmatic Interfaces
elements.description: The capability to interact with external systems through non-graphical, programmatic interfaces, such as APIs, SDKs, and backend services, to exchange data or trigger actions as part of task execution. This includes calling REST or GraphQL APIs, invoking cloud services, publishing or consuming messages from queues or event streams, and performing operations such as code pushes, data updates, or system integrations across enterprise platforms. This includes sending and receiving email, chat, or other messages through an API or mail protocol, including when those messages are also Official Communication (CAP-05).

elements.name: Code Execution
elements.description: The capability to write, execute, and debug code in various programming languages to automate tasks or solve computational problems. This includes implementing algorithms, writing scripts, compiling and running code, debugging errors, and integrating with external systems through APIs or backend services.

elements.name: File and Data Management
elements.description: The capability to manage the full lifecycle of files and data by creating, reading, modifying, organizing, converting, querying, and updating information across both unstructured artifacts (e.g. documents, spreadsheets, media files) and structured data stores (e.g. SQL/NoSQL databases, data warehouses, vector or embedding stores) in support of operational tasks. This includes ingesting and transforming datasets, generating or updating files, maintaining directory or schema structures, executing database queries or updates, and storing or retrieving embeddings or derived data products.

elements.name: System Management
elements.description: The capability to directly manage and configure technical systems and infrastructure by adjusting system settings, controlling computing resources, and administering operational environments across on-premise or cloud platforms. This includes monitoring system health and performance, managing authentication credentials and access controls, provisioning or scaling compute and storage resources, configuring operating system or runtime parameters, and applying system-level optimisations to support reliable operation.

lethal-trifecta.name: Lethal trifecta
lethal-trifecta.description: An agent that reads untrusted content, can reach sensitive data, and can send data out can be turned into an exfiltration channel by a single injected instruction. No one of the three creates the exposure; the three together do.

untrusted-content.name: Untrusted content
untrusted-content.description: Content that someone outside the organisation's control can write reaches the agent.
untrusted-content.question: Can anyone outside your organisation's control write content that this system reads?

CAP-02.note: Yes if it takes output from agents that other parties operate, or from agents that read untrusted content themselves.

CAP-04.note: Yes if its users are members of the public, or can upload or paste documents, images, or audio that someone else wrote.

CAP-05.note: Yes if it also reads replies or other inbound messages on the channels it sends through.

CAP-07.note: Web pages and search results can be written by anyone.

CAP-08.note: Whatever appears on screen reaches the agent, including web pages, emails, and documents written by others.

CAP-09.note: Yes if any API, queue, or mailbox it reads carries content from outside parties, such as inbound email, support tickets, form submissions, or webhooks.

CAP-10.note: Yes if it runs or reads code, packages, or repositories that outside parties can change.

CAP-11.note: Yes if any file or data store it reads holds content from outside parties, such as uploads, shared drives, or records created from customer input.

sensitive-data.name: Sensitive data
sensitive-data.description: The agent can read data that would cause harm if it left the organisation, such as personal data, credentials, or confidential records.
sensitive-data.question: Can this system read anything your organisation would not publish?

CAP-06.note: Yes if it holds payment credentials, or can read account, order, or customer records.

CAP-08.note: It can see whatever the signed-in user can open on the machine.

CAP-09.note: Yes if any API it can call returns personal, confidential, or credential data.

CAP-11.note: It reads the organisation's files, databases, or knowledge bases.

CAP-12.note: System administration reaches configuration, credentials, and logs.

outbound-channel.name: Outbound channel
outbound-channel.description: The agent can cause data to reach a destination outside the organisation's control.
outbound-channel.question: Can this system cause data to reach a destination your organisation does not control?

CAP-02.note: Yes if it can pass data to an agent that another party operates, or to an agent that has an outbound channel of its own.

CAP-04.note: Yes if its output is shown to people outside the organisation, or is rendered in a way that loads external images or links.

CAP-05.note: It sends messages to people outside the organisation.

CAP-06.note: Transactions carry data to external parties in payment references, order details, and booking fields.

CAP-07.note: Any request to a web address can carry data in the URL or the query.

CAP-08.note: It can use any application on the machine that sends data, including the browser and the mail client.

CAP-09.note: Yes if any API it can call writes to a system outside the organisation, or accepts a destination that the agent chooses.

CAP-10.note: Yes if the environment its code runs in can make network requests.

CAP-12.note: Yes if it can change network, sharing, or access settings so that data becomes reachable from outside.

oversight-within-reach.name: Oversight within reach
oversight-within-reach.description: An agent that can change the logs, monitors, permissions, or approvals that govern it holds both sides of a check. It can remove the check in pursuit of its task, or be told to by injected content.

own-safeguards.name: Its own safeguards
own-safeguards.description: The agent can change the logs, monitors, permissions, approval settings, or configuration that are meant to constrain it.
own-safeguards.question: Can any identity, tool, or code path the agent has write to what governs the agent itself?

CAP-08.note: Yes if it can open the settings of the application or platform that runs it.

CAP-10.note: Yes if code it runs can reach the files, services, or settings that hold its permissions, approvals, logs, or monitors.

CAP-11.note: Yes if its write access covers its own instruction, configuration, or log files.

CAP-12.note: It manages access controls, monitoring, and configuration, which can include its own.

any.note: The system has every capability held by an agent it can delegate to, including agents that another party operates. List those agents and their capabilities.

CAP-07.note: Yes if a browser is installed on the machine it operates.

CAP-09.note: Yes if the machine has applications or a terminal that call other systems.

CAP-10.note: Yes if it can open a terminal, a code editor, or any application that runs scripts.

CAP-11.note: It can open, change, and delete whatever files the signed-in user can.

CAP-12.note: Yes if the signed-in user can change system settings or access controls.

CAP-09.note: Yes unless the environment its code runs in blocks network access.

CAP-11.note: Code can read and write whatever files the account it runs under can.

CAP-12.note: Yes if credentials for infrastructure, deployment, or administration are within reach of the code it runs.

CAP-11.note: Yes if it can grant itself access to data stores it was not given.

retired.statement: Data exfiltration through message and API channels
Require human approval before executing high-impact actions
Use only MCP servers from verified and trusted developers
